endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Payors should always make determinations based on particular patient care needs and not base decisions on algorithms developed on “similar” or “like” patients.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Access to patient medical data, communication with payer treatment guidelines, human review and decision-making.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether basing AI-assisted coverage and prior-authorization decisions on current evidence-based criteria and individual patient circumstances, with criteria visible in clinician workflow, changes denial accuracy or patient outcomes. Support for R502 rests on two endorsements, one guidance document and one framework, and no supplied study documents the hazard of algorithmic denials either.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no test exists. The two endorsements express expert agreement, which a methodologist treats as opinion rather than evidence of effect.

The augmented intelligence principles state that payors should decide on particular patient care needs rather than on algorithms built from similar patients. The CHAI guide describes access to patient data, communication of payer treatment guidelines, and human review. Neither source reports measured compliance or outcomes, so the recommendation currently rests on professional guidance alone.

The CHAI guide lists human review and decision-making as part of the coverage process, which aligns with patients' interest in reaching a person when a claim is denied. No supplied study measures whether patients actually receive individualized review or whether accessible criteria reduce inappropriate denials.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI-assisted prior-authorization programs using current evidence-based criteria and individual patient review against programs without these features, measuring inappropriate denial rates, overturn rates on appeal, time to treatment, clinician burden, and patient harm. Studies should also test whether displaying payer criteria inside the clinician workflow changes submission completeness and approval accuracy.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether individualized, criteria-based AI coverage review performs equally across these groups, whose members may face higher administrative barriers when appealing denials.
